chunk_text: Lesson-01: What is a Sentence? A sentence is a group of words which gives a complete sense and has a subject and a finite verb. The words of a sentence must (1) give a complete sense — 'আকাঙ্ক্ষা' (e.g. 'I want some money.' / 'Ms Tania is an MA.' give complete sense; 'I want.' / 'Ms Tania is.' do not); (2) be orderly arranged — 'আসত্তি' (e.g. 'Roudiya is a brave girl.' / 'Abid looks handsome.' are orderly; 'Girl is a Roudiya brave.' / 'Looks handsome Abid.' are not); (3) be contextual — 'যোগ্যতা' (e.g. 'Birds fly in the sky.' is contextual; 'The cow flies in the sky.' is not). Single-worded Sentence: usually only a verb, part of Imperative sentence — Do./Come./Go./Stop./Halt. A single-worded sentence can also be without a verb — Yes./No./Thanks. Multi-worded sentence: usually has a subject and a verb; sometimes without a verb (e.g. 'Reading newspaper, Mom.' / '7 days only.' / 'No, not yet.' / 'Not at all.'). A sentence is the largest Grammatical unit; it is usually formed with a Subject, a finite verb and an object or a complement. The first word of a sentence begins with a capital letter and the sentence ends with a full stop (.), a question mark (?) or a note of exclamation (!) — e.g. 'The earth moves round the sun.' / 'What is your name?' / 'How sweetly she sings!'

chunk_text: Lesson-02: Parts of Sentence. A sentence has two parts: i. Subject (উদ্দেশ্য) ii. Predicate (বিধেয়). The Subject is a word or a group of words which tells who or what does something — the person or thing about whom the sentence is formed or written. The Predicate says something about the Subject; it is formed with the verb or with the verb and the rest of the sentence. To find the subject, separate the verb first and ask 'who' or 'what' before it; the answer is the subject. Example: 'The audience littered the theatre floor with torn wrappings and spilled popcorn.' The verb is 'littered'; who littered? — The audience did. So 'The audience' is the subject. What about the audience? — It (The audience) 'littered the theatre floor with torn wrappings and spilled popcorn.' The underlined part is the Predicate. Subject: the part of a sentence in which we mention the name of a person or a thing; the Subject is usually formed with a noun or round a noun. Predicate: the part of a sentence which says something about the work of the Subject; it is formed with a verb or with a verb and the rest of the sentence.

chunk_text: Lesson-02: Position of Subject and Predicate | Subject ও Predicate এর অবস্থান. 1. The Subject usually sits first in the sentence and the Predicate after it. But sometimes, to give emphasis to a special part of the sentence, the whole Predicate with the verb sits first in the sentence; then the meaning of the sentence changes slightly. E.g. 'The Titanic went down.' (Subject: The Titanic; Predicate: went down.) / 'The uses of adversity are sweet.' (Subject: The uses of adversity; Predicate: are sweet.) The same sentences with Subject and Predicate positions changed: 'Down went the Titanic.' (Predicate: Down went; Subject: the Titanic.) / 'Sweet are the uses of adversity.' (Predicate: Sweet are; Subject: the uses of adversity.) 2. In an Imperative Sentence the Second Person Subject 'You' is hidden. E.g. '(You) Do the work.' / '(You) Go there.' Compound Subjects and Compound Predicates: some sentences have two or more subjects or predicates, and each set of them is joined by a conjunction. If a sentence has two or more subjects, that subject is called a compound subject; if it has two or more predicates, that predicate is called a compound predicate. E.g. i. 'Raju and Saju are funny guys.' (compound subject: Raju and Saju) ii. 'Eating burger and swimming laps together may cause trouble.' (compound subject: Eating burger and swimming laps — two gerund phrases joined by 'and') iii. 'Meena enjoys cycling but loves swimming.' (compound predicate: enjoys cycling but loves swimming) iv. 'My pet sleeps on a couch and eats from a bowl.' (compound predicate: sleeps on a couch and eats from a bowl)

Assertive — Statement; 2. Interrogative — Question; 3. Imperative — Command/Request; 4. Optative — Desire/Prayer; 5. Exclamatory — Motion [as printed in the flow chart; intended 'Emotion']. According to structure: 1. Simple; 2. Complex; 3. Compound. Classes of Sentence: According to Meaning. Examples: 'I have to go to Ariq's house.' — Affirmative statement; 'You cannot go out now.' — Negative statement; both are Assertive Sentence. 'Did Minhaz ring you?' — Interrogative sentence. 'Don't be late.' — Imperative sentence. 'So nice of you, Mom!' — Exclamatory sentence. 'God bless you.' — Optative sentence. chunk_text: Lesson-03: 1. Assertive Sentence (বিবৃতিমূলক বাক্য). An assertive sentence is used to state facts, history, incidents, opinions, events, feelings, beliefs, etc. This sentence usually ends with a full stop. Example: She writes a diary. Structure: Subject (She) + Verb (writes) + Object (a diary) + . (full stop). Classification: Assertive or Statement sentence can be presented in three ways: i. Affirmative (হ্যাঁ-বোধক) ii. Negative (না-বোধক) iii. Emphatic (জোরালো রূপ). Negative and Emphatic statements are made by putting do (do/ does/ did) before the main verb of Simple present/ Simple past tense statements. Affirmative / Negative / Emphatic table: 'I like fish.' / 'I do not like fish.' / 'I do like fish.'; 'He loves her.' / 'He does not love her.' / 'He does love her.'; 'She cooked rice.' / 'She did not cook rice.' / 'She did cook rice.'; 'I have a car.' / "I don't have a car." / 'I do have a car.' Structures: Structure-1: Subject + 'to be' verb + extension (.) — 'I am a student.' / 'We are friends.' Structure-2: Subject + 'to be' verb + not + extension (.) — 'I am not a student.' / 'They are not friends.' Structure-3: Subject + auxiliary verb + main verb + extension (.) — 'I am writing a paragraph.' / 'They have done it.' Structure-4: Subject + auxiliary verb + not + main verb + extension (.) — 'He is not going to school.' / 'We have not done it.' Negative can also be made without changing the meaning: (a) He is a poor man. → He is not a rich man. (b) You are an old man. → You are not a young man. (c) Selina is a good girl. → Selina is not a bad girl. (d) I shall always remember you. → I shall never forget you. (e) He goes to school. → Does he not go to school? (f) The tiger is a rare animal. → The tiger is not a common animal.

chunk_text: Lesson-03: 2. Interrogative Sentence (প্রশ্নবোধক বাক্য). An interrogative sentence is used to ask a question. When we need to know something, we use interrogative sentences. There are two types of questions: wh- questions and yes/no questions. In an interrogative sentence, the position of the auxiliary verb is always before the subject. A. Wh question: Example: Where do you live? Structure: Wh-word (Where) + Auxiliary verb (do) + Subject (you) + Main verb (live) + Question mark (?) B. If the Wh-word acts as the subject of the sentence, auxiliary verb is not used in the question. For example: Who helped you in doing your project work? Structure: Subject (Who) + verb (helped) + object (you) + …? C. Yes/no question: Example: Do you like plants? Structure: Auxiliary verb (Do) + Subject (you) + Main verb (like) + plants + Question mark (?) Classification: Interrogative sentence is of two kinds: i. Wh-questions ii. Yes/ No questions Or, Verbal questions. i. Wh-questions: questions beginning with a wh-word (who, what, when, which, where, why, whom, whose and how) are called Wh-questions; they cannot be answered with Yes/No, they must be answered in a full sentence. Structure-1: Wh-word + verb + subject + extension (?) — 'Why are you here?' / 'What is your name?' / 'Who are you?' Structure-2: Wh-word + auxiliary verb + subject + main verb + noun/ extension (?) — 'Where are you going now?' / 'Where will you go tomorrow?' / 'What are you doing here?' / 'What did he tell you?' / 'Where did you go yesterday?' ii. Yes/ No or Verbal questions: questions beginning with auxiliary verbs (do, did, am, is, are, was, were, have, has, had, shall, will, etc.) are called Yes/ No or Verbal questions; they are answered with Yes/No. Ques.: Do you like birds? Ans.: Yes, I do. Ques.: Are you going to market? Ans.: No, I am not. Structure-1: Auxiliary verb + subject + main verb + extension (?) — 'Are you going to market?' / 'Have you done your homework?' / 'Do you like birds?' / 'Is she beautiful?' Structure-2: 'To be' verb + Subject + extension/ 'To have' verb + Subject + extension (?) — 'Is it your mobile phone?' / 'Has he a bicycle?' / 'Was he there?' / 'Have you a motor bike?' Forms of Interrogative Sentence: i. Affirmative (হ্যাঁ-সূচক) ii. Negative (না-সূচক). An Affirmative Interrogative Sentence is made Negative by putting 'not' after the subject — 'Do they play tennis?' → 'Do they not play tennis?' But if the contraction form of 'not' is used, it sits with the auxiliary verb and before the subject: 'Isn't she beautiful?' / "Don't you play cricket?" / "Can't you lift this box?" / "Didn't you go there?" Textbook Focus (EFT Page-35, 4.4) — AFFIRMATIVE & ENGATIVE SENTENCE [as printed; 'ENGATIVE' for 'NEGATIVE']: Affirmative sentence refers to something positive and does not contain any negative words (Example: I can recite poems). Negative sentence refers to something negative; usually we use a negative sentence to deny or to disagree with something. A negative sentence contains no, not, never. (Example: I cannot swim.)

chunk_text: Lesson-03: 3. Imperative Sentence (অনুজ্ঞাসূচক বাক্য). A sentence by which an order, advice, request, proposal, prohibition, etc. is understood is called an Imperative Sentence. Examples: Do the work. (You do the work.) Go there. (You go there.) Note: In an Imperative sentence the subject 'you' is usually hidden. If a request is meant, Please/ Kindly etc. is placed at the beginning or the end of the sentence; but if 'please' sits at the end, a comma (,) must sit before it. E.g. 'Please give me some money.' / 'Kindly help him.' / 'Lend me your pen, please.' / 'Dear students, silence please.' Forms of Imperative Sentence: i. Affirmative ii. Negative iii. Emphatic. Affirmative / Negative / Emphatic table: 'Come here.' / "Don't come here." / 'Do come here.'; 'Beat the dog.' / "Don't beat the dog." / 'Do beat the dog.'; 'Call a taxi.' / "Don't call a taxi." / 'Do call a taxi.'; 'Please open the door.' / "Please don't open the door." / 'Please do open the door.' Remember: i. To form a Negative imperative, 'Do not' must sit at the beginning of the sentence. ii. To form an Imperative Emphatic, 'Do' is used — 'See a doctor.' → 'Do see a doctor.' iii. If the subject of an Imperative sentence is 1st or 3rd person, the sentence begins with 'let' and the objective form of the subject sits after 'let' — 'Let us go out for a walk.' / 'Let him do the work.' iv. Many times 'Would you' or 'Could you' is used at the beginning of a sentence to express a request in the form of a question — 'Would you mind closing the door?' / 'Could you lend me some money, please?'

chunk_text: Lesson-03: 4. Optative Sentence (ইচ্ছা বা আশীর্বাদসূচক বাক্য). A sentence by which a prayer, blessing or wish is expressed is called an Optative Sentence. An Optative sentence usually begins with 'May' and a full stop sits at its end. Structure: May + Subject + Verb + Extension (.) Examples: 'May Allah help you.' / 'May your brother pass the exam.' / 'May he be happy.' / 'May Allah bless you.' / 'May Bangladesh prosper day by day.' Many times 'may' is hidden in this kind of sentence — 'Long live our president.' 5. Exclamatory Sentence (আবেগসূচক বাক্য). A sentence in which a sudden emotion or feeling of the mind is expressed is called an Exclamatory Sentence. Examples: 'Hurrah! We have won the game.' / 'Alas! My mother is dead.' / 'Bravo! You have killed the tiger.' Basically the forceful form (forceful vession — as printed) of an Assertive sentence is the Exclamatory sentence. In some cases an Exclamatory Sentence is formed by putting How and What at the beginning; in such cases How and What mean very, much, great, etc. E.g. 'How beautiful the garden is!' / 'What a fool I am!' / 'What a dangerous thing a little learning is!' / 'How lovely the flower is!' Remember: i. If a sentence begins with What/ How, a Note of exclamation (!) sits at the end of the sentence; and if a sentence begins with Hurrah/ Alas, a Note of Exclamation (!) sits after Hurrah/ Alas. ii. An Adjective or Adverb can sit directly after How; but a/ an joins after What. iii. Exclamatory Sentence can also be formed with If/ Had — 'If I were a rich man!' / 'Had I been a bird!'

chunk_text: Lesson-03: Classes of Sentence: According to Structure | গঠনভেদে বাক্যের শ্রেণিবিভাগ. Sentences are of three kinds according to Grammar rules and Structure: 1. Simple Sentence (সরল বাক্য) 2. Complex Sentence (জটিল বাক্য) 3. Compound Sentence (মিশ্র/ যৌগিক বাক্য). Examples: 'The cow eats grass.' / 'We have a car that is red in colour.' / 'He came to me and gave me a letter.' The first sentence has one Subject and one finite verb (সমাপিকা ক্রিয়া) — it is a simple sentence. The second sentence has one principal clause and one sub-ordinate clause — it is a complex sentence. The third sentence has two principal clauses joined by one co-ordinating conjunction — it is a compound sentence. 1. Simple Sentence: a sentence which has one Subject and one Finite Verb (প্রকাশিত বা উহ্য) is called a Simple Sentence. E.g. 'They play football.' (They = Subject, play = Finite Verb). Features of Simple Sentence: i. Many times the subjects of two Simple Sentences can be joined by a conjunction to make one simple sentence — and, but, both … and, either … or, neither … nor, not only … but also. E.g. 'Shakib plays cricket. His friends play cricket.' → 'Shakib and his friends play cricket.'; 'Shakib plays cricket. His friends don't play cricket.' → 'Shakib but not his friends play cricket.'; 'Shakib plays cricket. His friends also play cricket.' → 'Both Shakib and his friends play cricket.' ii. The subjects of two Simple Sentences can also be joined by and, but, both … and etc. to make one Simple sentence — 'I greeted my uncle. I greeted my aunt.' → 'I greeted both my uncle and aunt.' iii. The Adjective complements of two Simple Sentences can also be joined to make one Simple sentence — "It wasn't cold. It wasn't wet." → 'It was neither cold nor wet.' 2. Complex Sentence: a sentence which has one Principal Clause and one or more Subordinate Clauses is called a Complex Sentence. E.g. 'He said that he bought a book.' ('He said' = Principal Clause; 'that he bought a book' = Subordinate Clause). More Examples: 'I know the man who came here.' (Principal Clause: I know the man; Subordinate Clause: who came here; Finite Verbs: know, came; Subordinate Conjunction: who); 'When you reach there you will find a boy who helped us.' (Subordinate Clause: When you reach there; Principal Clause: you will find a boy; Subordinate Clause: who helped us; Finite Verbs: reach, will find, helped; Subordinate Conjunctions: when, who). Note: If a Complex sentence begins with an Independent/ Principal clause, no comma (,) sits between the clauses. But if the Complex sentence begins with a Subordinate/ Dependent clause, a comma (,) must sit after the Subordinate clause — 'I shall go if you come.' (Principal clause) / 'If you come, I shall go.' (Subordinate clause). 3. Compound Sentence: when a sentence has more than one Principal clause joined by a Coordinating Conjunction, it is called a Compound Sentence. E.g. 'I went to Dhaka and met my uncle.' ('I went to Dhaka' and 'I met my uncle' are two Principal Clauses joined by 'and'). More Examples: 'He is strong but I am weak.' (Finite Verbs: is, am; Coordinating Conjunction: but); 'Do it or leave the place.' (Finite Verbs: do, leave; Coordinating Conjunction: or). Note: If the Subject of a Compound Sentence joined by 'and' is the same, the Subject is not repeated after 'and'.

chunk_text: Lesson-02: 1. Noun | বিশেষ্য. Look at the sentences: 'The Padma is a big river.' (Padma: name of a river) / 'Dhaka is the capital of Bangladesh.' (Dhaka: name of a place) / 'Iron is a useful metal.' (Iron: name of a metallic substance) / 'The dog is a faithful animal.' (dog: name of a class of animal) / 'January is the first month of the year.' (January: name of a month) / 'Truthfulness is a great virtue.' (Truthfulness: name of a kind of human quality) / 'Water has no colour.' (Water: name of a kind of liquid substance). The words above express the name of one class or another. Although all nouns cannot be put into the above classes, most nouns can be classified this way. The purpose of classification is to help identify nouns. Without identifying the Noun, it is difficult to understand and make sentences. This kind of naming word (naming words) is called Noun or বিশেষ্য. Definition: The word by which the name of a person, thing, animal, place, substance, a group of something, a state or a quality is understood is called a Noun. In short, the name of anything is called Noun. (A noun is the name of anything.) 2. Pronoun | সর্বনাম. Look at the sentences: 1. 'Hasan is reading a book. It is very interesting.' 2. 'Students of this school are very disciplined. They all stay in the hostel.' 3. 'The officer asked soldiers to go to the field in the morning. But nobody was there.' In the sentences above, 'It' refers to 'book', 'they' refers to 'students' and 'nobody' refers to 'soldiers'. Here it, they and nobody are called pronoun, because they are used in place of a noun. Definition: The word which sits in place of a Noun and refers to that Noun is called a Pronoun. A Pronoun has all the features of a Noun. It can work in a sentence as subject/ object/ complement. Pronouns are used to avoid repetition of the Noun. Difference between Noun and Pronoun: There is some difference between Pronoun and Noun. Before a Noun, an adjective and a determiner sit, but a pronoun cannot take any adjective or determiner. A Noun can take a prefix and a suffix, but a pronoun cannot. The structure of a Pronoun is fixed.

chunk_text: Lesson-02: 3. Adjectives | বিশেষণ. Look at the sentences: 'Dhaka is a big city.' / 'It is a small town.' / 'He is a clever boy.' / 'It is a new pen.' / 'The girl is beautiful.' / 'The garden is nice.' / 'The night is dark.' / 'It is a cool day.' In the sentences above, the Bold words are Adjective, because they describe the fault, quality, state, number of something (a noun) — big, small, clever, new, beautiful, nice, dark, cool — these Adjectives tell us how the nouns city, town, boy, pen, girl, garden, night and day are, i.e. they give extra information about the nouns. Definition: The word which expresses the fault, quality, state, number, quantity etc. of a Noun or Pronoun is called an Adjective. Adjectives are not affected by the number, gender or case of the noun, because the adjective is not controlled by the noun it modifies. An Adjective has comparative and superlative forms. E.g. good — better — best. 4. Verb | ক্রিয়া. Look at the sentences: 'She teaches us English.' → action; 'The accident happened at night.' → event; 'He is in poor health.' → state; 'He eats rice.' → action; 'He goes to school.' → action. The words written in bold face here are verb or ক্রিয়া. A Verb is the most important part of a sentence. Even a one-word sentence is formed only with a verb. E.g. Stop! Go, etc. A verb phrase can be formed with more than one word, even with four words. E.g. 'May have been playing, Would have been written', etc. Definition: The word or phrase which expresses a work, event or state is called a Verb.

chunk_text: Lesson-02: 5. Adverb | ক্রিয়া বিশেষণ. An Adverb mainly modifies a verb. But besides the verb it also modifies an adjective, noun, pronoun, another adverb and the whole phrase or sentence. E.g. 1. 'Baby Nazneen sang sweetly.' (modifies the Verb 'sang') 2. 'Sayeed was rather quiet.' (modifies the Adjective 'quiet') 3. 'He works extremely slowly.' (modifies the Adverb 'slowly') 4. 'It takes quite a lot of courage to jump from a plane.' (modifies the Noun phrase 'a lot of courage') 5. 'Almost everybody was late.' (modifies the Pronoun 'everybody') 6. "I am going for a jogging later so I don't want to eat anything now." (modifies the whole clause 'I am going for a jogging') 7. "Personally, I don't like it." (modifies the whole sentence 'I don't like it') In the sentences above, sweetly, rather, extremely, quite, almost, later, personally are used as adverbs. An Adverb also modifies a preposition and a conjunction sometimes. E.g. 8. 'The grapes are well within reach.' (modifies the Preposition 'within') 9. "They don't like me just because I suffer in silence." (modifies the Conjunction 'because') Definition: The word which generally adds extra information to the meaning of a verb, i.e. modifies the verb, is called an Adverb. Tips: Generally, if you ask a Verb How? Where? When? How often? To what extent? etc., the answer you get is an Adverb. Difference between Adjective and Adverb: Adjective and Adverb both work as modifier. An Adverb modifies all parts of speech except Interjection and is used to express time or place. But an Adjective does not modify any word except a noun and an adjective is not used to express time or place.

chunk_text: Lesson-02: 6. Preposition | পদান্বয়ী অব্যয়. 'Pre-' means 'পূর্বে' and 'Position' means 'অবস্থান'. So, the meaning of Preposition is 'পূর্বে অবস্থান'. We generally use a preposition before a noun or noun phrase, pronoun or gerund to express the relation of a person, thing or event. E.g. 1. 'I gave the pen to Sheena.' (Preposition + noun) 2. 'I gave it to her.' (Preposition + pronoun) 3. 'Sheena devotes her time to writing.' (Preposition + gerund). We also use a preposition before a noun or pronoun to express place, time, cause, purpose or means. E.g. 4. 'He lives in Dhaka.' (preposition + place) 5. 'I will meet you at 7 p.m.' (preposition + time) 6. 'You need to leave early in order to arrive on time.' (preposition + purpose). Definition: The word which sits before a Noun or Pronoun and indicates the relation of that Noun or Pronoun with another word in the Sentence is called a Preposition. A Preposition can consist of one or more words. E.g. at, in, on, to, with, for, by, of, off, from, after, about, among, before, upto, in spite of, etc. Difference between Preposition and Adverb Particle: A Preposition generally takes an object. So they are always related to a noun, noun phrase, pronoun or gerund. Some prepositions do not take any object in a sentence; they are closely related to the Verb. They work in the sentence as an adverb. They are called Adverb particles. E.g. about, above, before, off, by, down, in, over, round, up, etc. are used as adverb particles. Examples: 1. 'She drove round the city.' (round + object = preposition) / 'She drove round.' (no object = adverb particle) 2. "I won't go out before lunch." (Preposition) / 'I have read this book before.' (adverb particle).

chunk_text: Lesson-02: 7. Conjunction | সংযোজক অব্যয়. A Conjunction is a joining word. (Conjunctions are joiners.) The main work of these words is to join words, phrases and clauses. Look at the sentences: 'Biplob or Sohel will help you.' / 'He is poor but honest.' In the first Sentence, 'or' joins the two Nouns Biplob and Sohel, so it is a Conjunction. In the second sentence, the Conjunction 'but' joins the two Clauses 'he is poor' and 'he is honest', so it is a Conjunction. Definition: The word which joins two or more words or phrases or sentences is called a Conjunction. Words used as Conjunction: and, but, or, yet, either, neither, so, as, because, if, unless, whether, since, that, so that, in order that, until, before, after, as well as, etc. 8. Interjection | আবেগসূচক অব্যয়. An interjection has no role in forming a Sentence. In fact, even though it has no relation with the other words of the sentence, it is used inside the Sentence to express the emotion of the mind. chunk_text: Lesson-02: How to Identify Nouns. Test a word by putting an article before it: if the article + word combination makes sense, the word is a noun. (i) 'a delight' and 'the pride' make sense, so 'delight' and 'pride' are nouns. (ii) Test 'extension': 'an extension' makes sense — 'We have an extension of telephone line in our bedroom.' — so 'extension' is a noun. Test the adjective 'beautiful': 'a beautiful' makes no sense, so 'beautiful' is not a noun. Test the verb 'eat': 'an eat' makes no sense, so 'eat' is not a noun. So this test separates nouns from the other parts of speech. Again, note: in some sentences an adjective sits before the noun and modifies it. E.g. 'The large, round guava lay on the table.' Here the article 'the' sits before the adjective 'large', yet the sentence makes complete sense. To find the noun, test the words after the article one by one: 'the large' makes no sense, 'the round' makes no sense, 'the guava' makes sense — so the noun we were looking for is 'guava'.

chunk_text: Lesson-03: Functions of the Nouns. 1. A noun sits as the subject of the verb in a sentence [Subject (Noun) + verb + extension]. E.g. 'Sheena is a good girl.', 'The cow gives us milk.' 2. A noun sits as the object of a transitive verb. E.g. 'I eat a mango.', 'He sees a bird.' 3. A noun sits as the indirect object of a verb [Subject + Verb + Indirect object (I.O.) + Direct object (D.O.)]. E.g. 'Sheena gave me a book.', 'She sent her friend a telex.' 4. A noun sits as the object of a preposition (preposition + noun). E.g. 'The cat is fond of milk.' 5. A noun sits as a noun in apposition. E.g. 'Mr. Rahman, a university teacher, teaches his students sincerely.' Note: if a noun phrase used after a subject noun refers to that same noun and is not the main part of the sentence, it is called a noun in apposition. Four characteristics of Noun: (i) Gender — classification by sex; (ii) Number — how many persons or things; (iii) Person — relation with the speaker; (iv) Case — the grammatical relation of a noun or pronoun with the other words in the sentence.

chunk_text: Lesson-08: Forming Feminine from Masculine. Generally feminine gender is formed from masculine in three ways: (i) by using a different word, (ii) by adding 'ess' at the end of the masculine noun, (iii) by using the feminine form of the masculine part of a compound noun. Gender Change. 1. By using a different word: abbot — abbess, boy — girl, bull — cow, cock — hen, dog — bitch, drake — duck, father — mother, fox — vixen, gander — goose, gentleman — lady, brother — sister, buck — doe, bachelor — maid / spinster, bullock — heifer, boar — sow, drone — bee, tailor — seamstress, horse — mare, husband — wife, man — woman, monk — nun, nephew — niece, ram — ewe, sir — madam, son — daughter, uncle — aunt, lord — lady, king — queen, male — female, lad — lass, colt — filly, stag — hind, hart — roe, wizard — witch. 2. By adding 'ess' without changing the root: author — authoress, giant — giantess, count — countess, baron — baroness, host — hostess, heir — heiress, Jew — Jewess, manager — manageress, lion — lioness, poet — poetess, prince — princess, patron — patroness, priest — priestess, shepherd — shepherdess, steward — stewardess, tutor — tutoress. 3. By dropping the vowel at the end of the masculine noun and adding 'ess': actor — actress, conductor — conductress, benefactor — benefactress, director — directress, doctor — doctress, enchanter — enchantress, hunter — huntress, inspector — inspectress, instructor — instructress, tiger — tigress, negro — negress, songster — songstress, waiter — waitress, porter — portress. Remember: in English there are very few feminine forms of the (noun + -ess) type. Professional words are generally treated as Common Gender, and feminine forms like authoress, poetess, directress, inspectress are generally not used. E.g. 'She is the director of this institute. (not directress)', 'She is an inspector of police. (not inspectress)'. 4. Compound nouns changing the first part: boy-friend — girl-friend, bull-calf — cow-calf, buck-rabbit — doe-rabbit, brother-in-law — sister-in-law, son-in-law — daughter-in-law, he-goat — she-goat, billy-goat — nanny-goat, cock-sparrow — hen-sparrow, father-in-law — mother-in-law, man-servant — maid-servant. 5. chunk_text: Lesson-09: The Case. Look at the sentence: 'I gave her my book.' Here the subject 'I' does the work of the verb 'gave', so 'I' is in the Nominative or subject case. Again, the work of 'gave' falls on 'book', so the relation of 'book' with 'gave' is the Objective Case. Again, between 'my' and 'book' there is a relation of ownership, so 'my' is in the Possessive Case. Definition: the relation of a Noun or Pronoun with the other words in a sentence is called Case. Classification of Cases. Case is of four kinds: 1. Nominative case (কর্তৃকারক) 2. Objective case (কর্মকারক) 3. Vocative case (সম্বোধন কারক) 4. Possessive case (সম্বন্ধ পদ). 1. Nominative case: when a noun or pronoun is used as the subject of a sentence and does the work of the verb, it is called Nominative case. E.g. 'Raju plays cricket.' — 'Raju' is the subject doing 'play', so 'Raju' is Nominative. Asking the verb 'who' or 'what' gives the Nominative case. 2. Objective case: when a noun or pronoun is used as the object in a sentence, it is called Objective case. E.g. 'Raju plays cricket.' — asking 'play' what Raju does gives 'cricket', so 'cricket' is Objective case. Asking the verb 'what' or 'whom' gives the Objective case. 3. Vocative Case: when a noun is addressed to say something, that noun is in the Vocative case, also called Nominative of Address. E.g. 'Meena, can you give me a pen?' — 'Meena' is used in address, so 'Meena' is Vocative case. 4. Possessive case: the case by which the ownership or relation of a noun or pronoun with another person or thing is shown is called Possessive case. E.g. 'It is Raju's pen.' — adding ('s) to 'Raju' shows Raju is the owner of the pen, so 'Raju's' is Possessive case. Generally the possessive is formed by adding apostrophe and s ('s) or only an apostrophe (') at the end of a noun; besides, 'of' also forms the possessive case, and some pronouns and adjectives have a Possessive Case. Note the uses of different kinds of Possessive Case in the passage: 'We have a small farm in our village. My father and his friend Mr. Mrinal own the farm. The name of the farm is Muradnagar Motsho Khamar. My father's name is Alimuzzaman. Our farm is a fish farm. Many of our neighbours are employed in the farm. The customers are our village people, some nearby stores and also some big departmental stores in Dhaka city. All the members of our family work for our business. Mr. Mrinal's family is also spending much time for it. The condition of the business is really good. We are really proud of our business. Working for the growth of the business is the dream of mine. Our neighbours' families will be benefited by that.'

chunk_text: Lesson-09: Formation of Possessives. Rule-1: add apostrophe and s ('s) at the end of a singular noun to form the Possessive Case. E.g. 'Jony owns a car.' so 'It is Jony's car.'; 'Rahim's umbrella, Dog's tail, People's right to know.' Rule-2: if a plural noun ends in s, add only an apostrophe ('). This rule also applies to proper nouns. E.g. 'Mira is in the girls' hostel.', 'This is boys' bedroom.', 'Students' representatives met the Principal.', 'Lawyers' association protested against the administrative initiative.', 'The Jeffersons' yard is always beautifully landscaped.' Rule-3: if a plural noun does not end in s, add apostrophe + s ('s). E.g. 'This is the way to the men's room.', 'She got a job in the children's section of the library.' Rule-4: for lifeless things the possessive is formed with 'of'. E.g. 'The leg of the chair is broken.' — 'Chair's leg is broken' is not used. Rule-5: when a lifeless thing is personified, i.e. life is attributed to it, 's is added. E.g. 'Arab's heroes', 'Nature's laws', 'At death's door', 'At the country's call'. Rule-6: where there is more than one hissing sound, s is not added, only apostrophe comma (') is used. E.g. 'For conscience' sake', 'For goodness' sake', 'For justice' sake'. Exception: "Pity's sake". Rule-7: time, place, distance, weight etc. lifeless nouns take 's. E.g. 'He is on a three day's leave.', "Three pound's weight." Rule-8: sometimes 'of' is used before an animate noun to form the possessive. E.g. 'The legs of the elephant are thick.' Rule-9: to show one of many, apostrophe and s ('s) are often added. E.g. "A book of Hasan's. (Hasan has many books; this is one of them.)" but 'A book of Hasan. (one book of Hasan)'. Possessive Case of Pronoun & Adjective. Table-1: the possessive forms of pronouns by person — 1st person singular I / me / my-mine, plural we / us / our-ours; 2nd person singular you / you / your-yours, plural you / you / your-yours; 3rd person singular he/she/it / him/her/it / his/her-hers/its, plural they / them / their-theirs. Table-2: Possessive Adjective vs Possessive Pronoun — my / mine, his-her / his-hers, our / ours, your / yours, its / —, their / theirs. Possessive Adjective and Possessive Pronoun have the same meaning, but their use and position differ: a Possessive Adjective sits before a noun, a Possessive Pronoun sits after the verb, though a Possessive Pronoun can also be used as a subject. E.g. 'This is my book. (Possessive Adjective)', 'This book is mine. (Possessive Pronoun)', 'This is our school. (Possessive Adjective)', 'This school is ours. (Possessive Pronoun)'. A possessive pronoun can also sit at the start of a sentence as the subject: 'Ours is a school which is very good.' No apostrophe (') is used in a Possessive Adjective or Possessive Pronoun. Note the big difference between possessive 'its' and "it's" (with an apostrophe): Its — of it; It's = It is. Most students make mistakes in using these. Also, 'One' is a Possessive Pronoun and "One's" is a Possessive Adjective. Possessive Adjective and Possessive Pronoun come under the Genitive Case. Genitive Case: the case that shows a noun, pronoun or adjective qualifying another noun is called Genitive Case. It generally shows ownership, but it can also show the source or quality of something. E.g. 'I borrowed Sam's calculator. (Noun in Genitive Case)', 'Our new house is blue. (Pronoun in Genitive Case)'. Genitive Case and Possessive Case look the same because both show ownership, but although Possessive Case always shows ownership, Genitive Case does not always do so. E.g. "Suzie's toy is new. (here it is both Possessive and Genitive)" but "The men's clothing section is downstairs. (here 'clothing' is not the men's possession; it means 'clothing for men' — this is Genitive Case only.)"

chunk_text: Lesson-01: What is Pronoun? 'Pro' means 'in place of', 'in favour of' or 'acting as'. A Pronoun is a word used in place of a Noun or working like a Noun. Look at the sentences: 'Roudiya loves Saturday.' / 'It is the day she gets her pocket money.' Here 'Roudiya' is not repeated; the Pronoun 'she' is used in its place, and 'it' is used in place of 'Saturday'. The pronouns 'she' and 'it' stop the noun from being repeated again and again and make the sentence pleasant to hear. A Pronoun has no identity of its own; it takes its meaning from the context, generally from the word in whose place it sits. That word is called the Antecedent of the pronoun (পূর্ববর্তী / অনুগামী). In the example above, 'Roudiya' is the Antecedent of the Pronoun 'her' and 'Saturday' is the Antecedent of the Pronoun 'it'. Since a pronoun is used in place of a noun, it can play the same roles as a noun. Definition: the word used in place of a noun is called a Pronoun. (A pronoun is a word that takes the place of a noun.) [Textbook Focus: English For Today, Page-22 (3.3).] A pronoun is also a part of speech. It is used in place of a noun, e.g. we use 'she' for grandma, and 'it' for a pet. I, me, he, she, herself, you, it, that, they, each, few, many, who, whoever, whose, someone, everybody, etc. are some common pronouns we use every day.

chunk_text: Lesson-01: MORE ON PRONOUN. We have learnt that a pronoun sits in place of a noun, i.e. a pronoun is used in place of a noun or a group of words that works like a noun. Examples: (a) 'Jahid met Jahanara in Dhaka.' → 'He first saw her in a Chinese restaurant.' (b) 'Visitors descend on New York's Central Park.' → 'They swarm across it like locusts.' A Pronoun has three main forms: i. First person pronouns: I, me, my, mine, we, us, our, ours. ii. Second person pronouns: you, your, yours. iii. Third person pronoun: he, his, him, she, her, hers, it, its, they, them, their, theirs. Different kinds of pronouns are used differently. Personal pronoun: this kind of pronoun is used in place of the different persons, things, places, animals etc. around us. E.g. 'Myra (Rupom's kitten) looks cute, but he thinks she is evil.' Possessive pronoun: these show ownership (মালিকানা). No apostrophe is used with a possessive. E.g. 'Your painting is interesting, but I prefer hers.' Interrogative Pronoun: these are used to ask questions. E.g. 'Who loves cakes?' (as the subject of the verb, for a person); 'You saw whom?' / 'You went with whom?' (as the object of the verb and the preposition, for a person); 'Whose is this?' (to show possession, for a person or thing); 'What is that?' / 'Which is heavier?' (for an animal or a thing).

chunk_text: Lesson-02: Classification of Pronouns. On the basis of their use and difference, pronouns are divided into eight parts: 1. Personal Pronoun (ব্যক্তিবাচক সর্বনাম) 2. Demonstrative Pronoun (নির্দেশক সর্বনাম) 3. Interrogative Pronoun (প্রশ্নবোধক সর্বনাম) 4. Relative Pronoun (সম্বন্ধবাচক সর্বনাম) 5. Indefinite Pronoun (অনিশ্চয়তাবাচক / অনির্দিষ্ট সর্বনাম) 6. Distributive Pronoun (বণ্টন-নির্দেশক সর্বনাম) 7. Reflexive Pronoun (আত্ম-নির্দেশক সর্বনাম) 8. Reciprocal Pronoun (পারস্পরিক সম্পর্ক নির্দেশক সর্বনাম). How to Identify Pronouns (table): Personal Pronoun — sits in place of a person: I, we, you, he, she, it, they, etc. Demonstrative Pronoun — points out a noun in a special way: this, that, these, those, etc. Interrogative Pronoun — used to ask a question, sits at the start of the sentence: who, whose, whom, which and what. Relative Pronoun — establishes a relation between two sentences, sits inside the sentence: who, whose, which, whom, that, etc. Indefinite Pronoun — refers to an indefinite person or thing: any, one, anyone, some, someone, anybody, somebody, nobody, many, everyone, all, etc. Distributive Pronoun — refers to each person or thing of the same kind separately: each, every, either, neither, etc. Reflexive Pronoun — formed with self or selves, subject and object are the same person: myself, ourselves, yourself, yourselves, himself, herself, themselves, etc. Reciprocal Pronoun — shows a mutual relation between more than one person or thing: each other and one another.

chunk_text: Lesson-02: 1. Personal Pronoun | ব্যক্তিবাচক সর্বনাম. Definition: the Pronoun that sits in place of a person is called a Personal Pronoun. Examples: 1. 'I am a girl.' 2. 'He is a student.' 3. 'She is a teacher.' 4. 'We are boys.' In the sentences above, I, He, She and We are used in place of different persons, so they are Personal Pronouns. Personal Pronouns are of three kinds: 1. First Person — the person who speaks is the first person: I, we, me, us, my, our, etc. 2. Second Person — the person addressed is the Second Person: you, your, thou, thy, thee, etc. 3. Third Person — the person spoken about is the Third Person: He, she, they, him, her, them, their, it, its, etc. Forms of Personal Pronouns by Number, Gender and Case (tables): 1. First Person (Masculine or Feminine) — Nominative: I / We; Objective: Me / Us; Possessive: My / Our. 2. Second Person (Masculine or Feminine) — Nominative: You / You; Objective: You / You; Possessive: Your, Yours / Your, Yours. 3. Third Person (Masculine or Feminine or Neuter) — Nominative: He / She / It / They; Objective: Him / Her / It / Them; Possessive: His / Her / Its / Their, Theirs. Remember: (a) Most Personal Pronouns have two Possessive Case forms. Among them, my, our, they, your, her, their are Possessive Adjectives, because they sit before a noun and qualify it like an adjective. E.g. 'That is my book.', 'Her dress is old.', 'These are your shirts.' (b) mine, thine, hers, ours and theirs sit after the finite verb in the sentence and no noun sits after them that they could qualify, so these Possessive forms of the Personal pronoun are called Possessive Pronoun. E.g. 'This pen is mine.', 'That pencil is yours.', 'That ring is hers.' (c) 'His' can be both Possessive Adjective and Possessive Pronoun. E.g. 'This is his pen. (Possessive Adjective)' / 'This pen is his. (Possessive Pronoun)'. (d) 'Its' is used only as a Possessive Adjective. E.g. 'Its beak is sharp.', 'The jackal lost its tail.'

chunk_text: Lesson-02: Some uses of Personal Pronoun. i. Since a Personal Pronoun is used in place of a noun, its number, person and gender are the same as the noun's. E.g. 'Sheema has lost her watch.', 'Rana lends his book to me.' ii. In place of a Collective noun a singular number (Neuter gender) pronoun is used, and in place of a noun of multitude a plural number pronoun is used. E.g. 'The jury gave its unanimous opinion. (Collective noun)', 'The jury are divided in their opinions. (Noun of multitude)'. iii. If two or more nouns are joined by 'and', a plural pronoun is used in their place. E.g. 'Meena and Sheena learn their lessons regularly.' iv. If a first person is joined with another noun or pronoun, a first person plural pronoun is used in their place; and if a second person is present, a second person plural pronoun is used. E.g. 'He and I did our best. (his নয়)', 'You and your teammates are guilty for your failure. (their নয়)'. v. If 'each', 'every' or 'no' sits before two nouns joined by 'And', the pronoun is always singular. E.g. 'No man and no body has done his duty.' vi. Use of 'It': 'it' is used (i) in place of a lifeless thing — 'Here is your book, take it away.'; (ii) in place of an animal — 'It is my dog.'; (iii) in place of a small child — 'When I saw the baby, it was crying.'; (iv) to refer to a previous statement — 'He was honest and we know it.'; (v) as a Preparatory or Provisional subject before the verb 'to be' — 'It is certain that you are wrong.'; (vi) to emphasise a later noun or pronoun — 'It is the book that I want.'; (vii) as the subject of an impersonal verb — 'It rains.'; (viii) to speak of weather or time — 'It is fine today.', 'It is 7 o'clock.'; (ix) in place of a collective noun — 'The jury agrees in its opinion.'

chunk_text: Lesson-02: 2. Demonstrative Pronoun | নির্দেশবাচক সর্বনাম. Definition: the Pronouns that sit in place of one or more persons or things and point them out are called Demonstrative Pronouns. Examples: i. 'This is his pen.' ii. 'These are her books.' iii. 'That is a bird.' iv. 'Those are flowers.' In the sentences above, This, These, That and Those sit in place of nouns (pen, books, bird, flowers) and point them out, so they are Demonstrative Pronouns. Use of 'This' and 'That' as Demonstrative Pronouns. The main work of Demonstratives is to point out the nearness or distance of a person or thing. i. 'This' points out one near person or thing and 'These' points out more than one near person or thing. E.g. 'This is my pen.', 'These are my pens.' ii. 'That' points out one distant person or thing and 'Those' points out more than one distant person or thing. E.g. 'This is my pen and that is yours.', 'These are my pens and those are hers.' iii. Sometimes 'this' and 'that' are used to emphasise. E.g. 'He must do the work and this at once.' iv. When comparing nouns of the same kind, 'that' and 'those of' (if plural) are used to avoid repeating an earlier noun. E.g. 'The rice of Barishal is better than that of Dinajpur. (The rice of নয়)', 'The mangoes of Rajshahi are tastier that those of Satkhira. (the mangoes of নয়)'. Note: some Demonstrative pronouns can be used in a sentence as adjectives; then they are called Demonstrative Adjectives. E.g. 1. 'This is a girl. (Demonstrative pronoun)' / 'I like this girl. (Demonstrative Adjective)'. 2. 'That is a beautiful girl. (Demonstrative Pronoun)' / 'That girl is beautiful. (Demonstrative Adjective)'.

chunk_text: Lesson-02: 3. Interrogative Pronoun | প্রশ্নবোধক সর্বনাম. Definition: the Pronoun used to ask a question is called an Interrogative Pronoun. There are only five Interrogative Pronouns: Who, Whom, Whose, What and Which. Remember: a verb is used after an Interrogative pronoun (not an adjective). Examples: 'Who has done the work?', 'Whom do you want?', 'Which is your brother?', 'What do you say?', 'Whose pen is this?' In the sentences above, who, whom, whose, which and what are used to ask questions, so they are Interrogative Pronouns. Among them, 'who' is used in place of a person, and its form changes in different cases: Nominative — Who (কে?), Objective — Whom (কাকে?), Possessive — Whose (কার?); e.g. 'Who did it?', 'Whom do you want?', 'Whose pen is it?' Use of Interrogative Pronouns. i. Who: only for a person (both Singular and Plural). E.g. 'Who is he?', 'Who are they?' ii. What: in place of a thing (both Singular and Plural) and to ask about a profession. E.g. 'What is your name?', 'What is your father?' iii. Which: for both person and thing (both Singular and Plural); Which expresses choosing one among many. E.g. 'Which is your book?', 'Which of the girls has done it?' iv. Whom: 'whom' is used in place of 'Who' as the object of a verb. E.g. 'Whom did they invite?' But in modern English 'whom' is used very little; as the object 'who' itself is used. E.g. 'Who did you invite to the party?' v. Whose: used to show whose ownership or right a person or thing is, to point to a person or thing, and to give extra information about a person or thing. E.g. 1. 'Whose house is that? (মালিকানা)' 2. "It's the house whose door is painted red." 3. 'Rana, whose brother he was, had heard the joke before.'

chunk_text: Lesson-02: 4. Relative Pronoun | সম্বন্ধবাচক সর্বনাম. Definition: the Pronoun that is used in place of a previously mentioned Noun, points to it, and joins two Sentences like a Conjunction is called a Relative Pronoun. Examples: 'I know the man who came here last night. (A man came here last night. I know the man.)', 'This is the pen that/ which I lost yesterday.', 'These are the books which have just arrived.' In the first sentence, 'who' does two jobs at once: i. it sits in place of the noun 'man' and points to it, so it is a Pronoun; ii. like a Conjunction it joins two sentences, so 'who' is also called a conjunctional pronoun — but we generally call 'who' a Relative Pronoun. In the same way, 'that' and 'which' in the second and third sentences are Relative Pronouns. 5. Indefinite Pronoun | অনির্দিষ্ট সর্বনাম. Definition: the Pronoun that does not point to any definite person or thing but refers to an indefinite person or thing is called an Indefinite Pronoun. Examples: 'One should obey one's parents.', 'Some of the boys have passed in the examination.', 'Any of the books can help you.', 'Somebody has done this.', 'Always try to do good to others.', 'One cannot please everybody.' In the sentences above, one, some, any, somebody and others do not refer to any definite person or thing but to indefinite persons or things, so they are Indefinite Pronouns. Some uses of Indefinite Pronouns. One: when 'One' is the subject of a sentence, 'one's' is used in its place in the possessive case, not his or him. E.g. "One should respect one's superiors." But if 'every', 'no' or some phrase sits before 'One', then he, his, him etc. are used. 'One', 'everyone', 'no one' etc. refer to indefinite persons. E.g. 'Everyone should do his duty.' One of: 'one of' means one person, one thing or one of a class among many. A plural noun sits after it, but the verb is always singular. E.g. 'One of my friends is ill.' Others: 'Others' always sits in place of a person, never in place of a thing or place. E.g. 'Reena, Sheena and others were present in the party.'

chunk_text: Lesson-02: 6. Distributive Pronoun | বিভাজক সর্বনাম. Definition: the Pronoun that points to each of two or more persons or things separately is called a Distributive Pronoun. Examples: 'Each of the boys got a prize.', 'Either of the two books will do.', 'Neither of these two boys is honest.', 'None of my four friends came.' In the sentences above, each (each of the boys), either (one of the two books), neither (neither of the two boys), none (nobody) do not refer to all persons or things together but to each separately, so they are Distributive Pronouns. Some uses of Distributive Pronouns. i. Each: 'each' is used to separate each of two or more persons or things. E.g. 'Each of us was present in his class.', 'Each of the two boys has done this.' ii. Either: 'either' is used to show one of two persons or things as separate from the other. E.g. 'Either Selina or Sumi is guilty.', 'Either of the two boys has done this.' iii. Neither: 'neither' is the negative form of 'either'. It is used to show that neither of the two is so. E.g. 'Neither of the two boys is present.', 'Neither of the two pens is good.' 7. Reflexive Pronoun | আত্মবাচক সর্বনাম. Definition: when a Pronoun formed by joining -self or -selves to a Personal Pronoun is used as the Object and points to the previous Subject, it is called a Reflexive Pronoun. In other words, when the subject itself works as the subject and the object of the verb, it is called a Reflexive Pronoun. Examples: 'I did it myself.', 'She cooked food herself.', 'They made the house themselves.' In the sentences above, myself, herself, themselves etc. are the objects of the verbs do, cook, make, and each of them again points to the previous subject; the subject and the object of the sentence are the same person, so they are Reflexive pronouns. Form of reflexive pronouns: a Reflexive pronoun is basically a compound word of a possessive adjective + -self. E.g. myself, yourself etc. Besides, an object pronoun + -self can also form a reflexive. E.g. himself. Table: Singular — My + self = Myself, Your + self = Yourself, Him/Her/It + self = Himself / Herself / Itself; Plural — Our + selves = Ourselves, Your + selves = Yourselves, Them + selves = Themselves. What is an Emphatic Pronoun? When a Reflexive Pronoun sits after a Noun or pronoun, points to it and puts emphasis on it, it is called an Emphatic pronoun. E.g. 'I myself went there.', 'They themselves arranged the party.' Although they look the same, Reflexive and Emphatic Pronouns differ in meaning and use. A Reflexive Pronoun is used as the Object of a sentence, so it cannot be removed. But an Emphatic Pronoun is used to put emphasis on the Subject, so even if it is removed the Sentence does not become wrong. An Emphatic Pronoun sits immediately after the Noun on which it puts emphasis. E.g. 'We talked to the headmaster himself.'

chunk_text: Lesson-02: 8. Reciprocal Pronoun | পরস্পর সম্বন্ধবাচক সর্বনাম. Definition: the Pronoun that shows a mutual relation between two or more persons is called a Reciprocal Pronoun. Examples: 'The two boys helped each other.', 'They fought one another.' In the two sentences above, 'each other' and 'one another' show a mutual relation between two or more than two persons, so they are Reciprocal Pronouns. Note: to show a relation between two persons 'each other' is used, and to show a relation between more than two persons 'one another' is used.

chunk_text: Lesson-03: Person. Person is a grammatical term; it shows what relation a noun has with the speaker. Person tells whether the speaker is speaking about himself, addressing someone, or speaking about someone. Person is of three kinds — First, Second and Third. When the Person changes, the form of the noun does not change. Examples: 'I go to school with you.', 'He reads in class six.', 'She is a good girl.', 'They play cricket.', 'You are my friend.', 'This is our house.' In the sentences above, I, you, he, she, they, my, our etc. words are sometimes used as subject and sometimes as object to point to a Noun or Pronoun; these words are Person. The use of the verb in a sentence depends on the use of person; with different persons the verb is also used differently. E.g. 'I play.' / 'You play.' / 'He/ She plays.'; 'I go.' / 'You go.' / 'He/ She goes.' Definition: the subjects on which the verb in different Sentences depends to complete its work are called Person. Classification of Person | Person-এর শ্রেণিবিভাগ. In English Person is of three kinds: i. First Person (উত্তম পুরুষ) ii. Second Person (মধ্যম পুরুষ) iii. Third Person (নাম পুরুষ). Table: 1st person — Singular I (আমি), Plural We (আমরা); 2nd person — Singular You (তুমি), Plural You (তোমরা); 3rd person — Singular He [সে (পুং)], She [সে (স্ত্রী)], It (ইহা), Plural They (তারা, ইহারা). i. First Person: the person by which the speaker expresses himself or themselves is called First Person. E.g. I, we, me, us, our, my, mine, ours, etc. Examples: 'I go.', 'We go.', 'Our home.' ii. Second Person: the person to whom something is said in a sentence is called Second Person. E.g. You, your, thou, thee, etc. Examples: 'You go.', 'Your home.' iii. Third Person: the person about whom something is said in a sentence is called Third Person. E.g. He, she, him, her, his, they, it, Rony, Sunny, Meena, etc. Examples: 'He goes.', 'She goes.', 'Roney goes.', 'They go.' The six personal pronouns in the table above are used as subject. They have three more forms: i. Object ii. Possessive iii. Double possessive. Table: 1st person singular — Subject I, Object me, Possessive/Double possessive my — mine; 1st person plural — Subject we, Object us, Possessive/Double possessive our — ours; 2nd person singular — Subject you, Object you, Possessive/Double possessive your — yours; 2nd person plural — Subject you, Object you, Possessive/Double possessive your — yours; 3rd person singular — Subject he, Object him, Possessive/Double possessive his; Subject she, Object her, Possessive/Double possessive her — hers; Subject it, Object it, Possessive/Double possessive its; 3rd person plural — Subject they, Object them, Possessive/Double possessive their — theirs.

chunk_text: Lesson-01: What is Adjectives? Read the passage and notice the underlined words: 'Mr. Haque is a happy (সুখী) man. He has an intelligent (বুদ্ধিমতী) wife. They have three children. All of them are bright students. They are gentle and polite. Their parents are proud of them. They come of a rich family but they are not arrogant (অহংকারী) in their attitude.' If you notice, the underlined words describe (বর্ণনা) or qualify (বৈশিষ্ট্যযুক্ত) or modify (বিশেষিত) a noun or pronoun. For example, 'happy' shows Mr. Haque as 'সুখী', 'intelligent' shows the quality of his wife. So happy, intelligent and the underlined words in the passage are adjectives. Thus we see, an Adjective gives extra information about a noun or pronoun. The things an Adjective usually tells us about are: Quality — a nice day, a beautiful girl; Size — a tall tree, a big car, a small boy; Age — a young man, an old house; Temperature — a cool morning, a hot day; Shape — a round table, a square room; Colour — black eyes, gray hair, a white dress; Origin — a Swiss watch, a Chinese phone. Definition (সংজ্ঞা): the word that shows the fault, quality, state, number, measure etc. of a Noun or Pronoun is called an Adjective. Before an Adjective an adverb of degree (intensifier) like too/ very can be used. E.g. 'She is too tired.', 'The rose is a very beautiful flower.' The degree of an Adjective is a very notable matter. Its natural degree, i.e. the base (মূল) form, is called Positive Degree. Besides, an adjective has Comparative and Superlative degree. These are not affected by number or gender or case, because they are not controlled by the Noun or Pronoun they modify.

chunk_text: Lesson-02: How to Identify Adjectives. The root part of a word is called the root. When certain suffixes are added to the end of a Root/ Word, an Adjective is formed. An Adjective can be recognised by these suffixes: -able/ -ible → acceptable, favourable, horrible. -al → accidental, casual, emotional. -an/ -ian → American, European, Indian. -ary/ -ory → momentary, reformatory. -atic/ -tic/ -ative → talkative, fantastic, fanatic. -en → bounden, golden, silken. -ern/ -ery → Eastern, Southern, Silvery. -ese → Chinese, Japanese. -ful → dutiful, useful, careful. -ial/ -ic/ -ical → partial, atomic, lyrical. -ish → bookish, childish, foolish, selfish. -ive → abusive, submissive. -less → artless, needless, hopeless. -ly → yearly, brotherly, cowardly. -ous → dangerous, famous, prosperous. -some → burdensome, troublesome. -t (ant/ -ent) → absent, eminent, innocent, tolerant. -tial → essential, influential, substantial. -worthy → noteworthy, blameworthy. -y → airy, bloody, cloudy, hilly.

chunk_text: Lesson-03: Position of Adjectives. 1. Attributive Position: Adjectives sit before the noun (adjective + noun). E.g. i. 'Meena is a good girl.' (adj. noun) ii. 'He is a wise man.' (adj. noun) 2. Predicative Position: this kind of adjective generally sits after the noun (noun + adjective). i. When more than one adjective is used to qualify one noun. E.g. 'The boys, thin and smart, brilliant and wise are invited to the party.' (noun, adj., adj.) ii. When an Adjective shows a number through a phrase. E.g. 'I want a boy ten years old.' (noun, adj.) iii. In poetry. E.g. 'Hearing which your blood will be cold.' (adj.) iv. When an Adjective is used to show a title. E.g. 'Omar, the great, was a just ruler.' (noun, adj.) Note: when an Adjective sits before a noun it is called a Pre-modifier, and when it sits after it is called a Post-modifier. 3. Adjective can also sit after an adverb. Structure: Adverb + Adjective + Noun. E.g. 'The rose is a very beautiful flower.' (adv. adj. noun) 'It is a very hot day.' (adv. adj. noun)

chunk_text: Lesson-04: Classification of Adjectives. Adjectives are mainly of four kinds: 1. Adjective of quality Or, Descriptive Adjective 2. Adjective of quantity Or, Quantitative Adjective 3. Adjective of number Or, Numeral Adjective 4. Pronominal Adjective. 1. Adjective of Quality (গুণবাচক বিশেষণ): it shows the fault, quality or state of a Noun. E.g. 'He is a good boy. Rahim is dull.', 'The woman is old. The farmer is poor.' In the sentences above, good, dull, old, poor etc. words show the quality, fault or state of the nouns boy, Rahim, woman, farmer, so they are Adjective of quality. 2. Adjective of Quantity (পরিমাণবাচক বিশেষণ): it shows the measure of a Noun. E.g. 'I have got some money.', 'Give me some milk.', 'There is little water in his glass.', 'He has enough time to walk.' In the sentences above, some, little, enough etc. words show the measure of the nouns money, water, milk, time, so they are Adjective of quantity. 3. Adjective of Number/ Numeral Adjective (সংখ্যাবাচক বিশেষণ): it shows the definite number, place or order of a Noun. E.g. 'I have five cars.', 'He is the first boy in the class.' In the first sentence 'five' shows the number of the noun 'car', and in the second sentence 'first' shows the place or order of the noun 'boy' according to the class, so 'five' and 'first' are Adjective of number. Adjective of Number can again be divided into three parts: Cardinal Numeral Adjective — One, two, three, four, etc.; Ordinal Numeral Adjective — First, second, third, etc.; Multiplicative Numeral Adjective — Single, double, triple, etc.

chunk_text: Lesson-04: 4. Pronominal Adjective (সর্বনাম বিষয়ক বিশেষণ): when a Pronoun sits before a Noun and is used as an Adjective, it is called a Pronominal Adjective. E.g. 'Some boys are playing. Every boy was given a prize. She likes this picture.' In the sentences above, some, every and this sit before the nouns boys, boy and picture and work like adjectives, so these pronouns are Pronominal Adjectives. Types of Pronominal Adjective: Pronominal Adjective is of 4 (four) kinds: (a) Demonstrative Adjective: the words that sit before a noun and point it out specially are called Demonstrative Adjectives. E.g. This, that, these, those, such, etc. Examples: 'This girl is intelligent. These cars are new. Those mangoes are tasty.' (b) Distributive Adjective: the Adjectives that show each of several persons or things separately are called Distributive Adjectives. E.g. every, each, either, neither, etc. Examples: 'They each have their own car. Every student in the class is capable of passing the exam. You can park on either side of the street.' (c) Interrogative Adjective: the Adjectives that are used to ask a question about a noun or pronoun are called Interrogative Adjectives. E.g. what, which, whose, etc. Examples: 'What vegetable do you like most? Which book do you need? Whose car is this?' (d) Possessive Adjective: the Adjectives that show right/ ownership or relation are called Possessive Adjectives. E.g. my, our, your, her, their, its, etc. Examples: 'Here is our house.', 'This is her bag.' Note: many times a Pronominal Adjective and a Pronoun look the same, but there is a difference between them. A Pronoun does the work of a Noun; and a Pronominal Adjective does the work of an Adjective. E.g. 'His room is clean. (Adjective)' / 'Ours is the best house in this area. (Pronoun)'. Remember, there is one more kind of Adjective, and that is Proper Adjective. These Adjectives are formed from a Proper Noun; especially they are formed from the names of geographical places (continents, countries, states). These Adjectives show origin or source. E.g. Japanese, Chinese, American, Canadian, Bangladeshi, Indian, etc.

chunk_text: Lesson-05: Degrees of Comparison (Comparison of Adjectives & Adverbs). Notice the underlined words in the sentences below: 'Mr. Karim is a very rich man. He is richer than his brother. He is the richest man in our village.' The examples above show three different uses of Adjective. In the first example 'rich' simply shows the state of a person, in the second example 'richer' shows comparison between two people, and in the third example 'the richest' shows one among many. This is Degrees of Comparison. In the examples, 'rich' is called Positive degree, 'richer' is called Comparative degree, and 'the richest' is called superlative degree. Box: Adjective that simply shows a state is its Positive degree. Adjective that shows comparison between two is its Comparative degree. Adjective that shows comparison with more than two or many is its Superlative degree. Illustration (diagram on the page, three girls): Positive — 'Rupa's hair is long.' Comparative — 'Meena's hair is longer.' Superlative — "Diana's hair is the longest." Again, notice the underlined words in the sentences below: 'Mina runs fast. She runs faster than Tina. She runs fastest of all the girls in the class.' The examples above show three different uses of Adverb. In the first example 'fast' simply shows 'how she runs', in the second example 'faster' shows comparison between two, and in the third example 'fastest' shows the state of 'how one runs' among many. This is Degrees of Adverb. In the examples above, 'fast' is positive degree, 'faster' is comparative degree, and 'fastest' is superlative degree. Definition (সংজ্ঞা): to show comparison between different persons, animals or things, the different forms (রূপান্তর) of Adjective and Adverb are called Degrees of comparison. It is also called Comparison of Adjectives or Adverbs. To show comparison, an Adjective or Adverb has three forms: 1. Positive Degree, 2. Comparative Degree and 3. Superlative Degree. 1. Positive Degree: when an Adjective or Adverb simply shows a quality without comparison, it is Positive Degree. E.g. 'Rahim is a good boy.', 'It is a tall tree.' 2. Comparative Degree: when an Adjective or Adverb shows comparison of quality between two, it is Comparative Degree. E.g. 'Abul is taller than Karim.', 'Rina is more intelligent than Sheela.' 3. Superlative Degree: when an Adjective/ Adverb shows comparison of quality among more than two, i.e. many, it is Superlative Degree. E.g. 'Hasan is the best boy in the class.', 'Mr Jamal is the wisest man in the village.'

chunk_text: Lesson-05: Comparison of Adjectives (rules 4-7). 4. If the Positive Degree ends in 'y' and there is a Vowel before it, 'er' is added to make Comparative Degree and 'est' to make Superlative Degree. E.g. gay (উৎফুল্ল) — gayer — gayest; gray/ grey (ধূসর) — grayer/ greyer — grayest/ greyest. 5. If the Adjective in Positive Degree ends in a single Consonant and there is a single Vowel before it, the last Consonant is doubled and then 'er' is added to make Comparative and 'est' to make Superlative Degree. E.g. Big (বড়) — bigger — biggest; Fat (মোটা) — fatter — fattest; Fit (যোগ্য) — fitter — fittest; glad (খুশি/ আনন্দিত) — gladder — gladdest; Hot (গরম) — hotter — hottest; Red (লাল) — redder — reddest; Sad (দুঃখিত) — sadder — saddest; Thin (পাতলা) — thinner — thinnest. 6. But if the Adjective ends in two Consonants or there are two vowels before the last Consonant, 'er' and 'est' are added as usual to make Comparative and Superlative Degree. E.g. broad (চওড়া) — broader — broadest; cool (শীতল) — cooler — coolest; green (সবুজ) — greener — greenest; mean (নীচ) — meaner — meanest; thick (পুরু) — thicker — thickest. 7. For Adjectives of two or more Syllables and Adjectives ending in 'ful', to show superiority 'more' or 'most' is placed before, and to show inferiority 'less' or 'least' is placed before, to form Comparative and Superlative Degree respectively. E.g. active (কর্মঠ) — more active / less active — most active / least active; attentive (মনোযোগী) — more attentive / less attentive — most attentive / least attentive; attractive (আকর্ষণীয়) — more attractive / less attractive — most attractive / least attractive; beautiful (সুন্দর) — more beautiful / less beautiful — most beautiful / least beautiful; careful (সতর্ক) — more careful / less careful — most careful / least careful; comfortable (আরামদায়ক) — more comfortable / less comfortable — most comfortable / least comfortable; dangerous (বিপজ্জনক) — more dangerous / less dangerous — most dangerous / least dangerous; difficult (কঠিন) — more difficult / less difficult — most difficult / least difficult; durable (টেকসই) — more durable / less durable — most durable / least durable; dutiful (কর্তব্যপরায়ণ) — more dutiful / less dutiful — most dutiful / least dutiful; famous (বিখ্যাত) — more famous / less famous — most famous / least famous; honest (সৎ) — more honest / less honest — most honest / least honest; hopeful (আশাবাদী) — more hopeful / less hopeful — most hopeful / least hopeful; important (গুরুত্বপূর্ণ) — more important / less important — most important / least important; industrious (পরিশ্রমী) — more industrious / less industrious — most industrious / least industrious; intelligent (বুদ্ধিমান) — more intelligent / less intelligent — most intelligent / least intelligent; obedient (অনুগত/ বাধ্যগত) — more obedient / less obedient — most obedient / least obedient; useful (উপকারী) — more useful / less useful — most useful / least useful.

chunk_text: Lesson-05: Comparison of Adverbs | Adverb-এর তুলনা. Like Adjectives, Adverbs also have Comparison of Degrees. 1. To some Adverbs 'er' is added to make Comparative and 'est' to make Superlative. E.g. fast — faster — fastest; hard — harder — hardest; quick — quicker — quickest; soon — sooner — soonest. 2. To Adverbs ending in -ly, 'more' is placed before to make comparative and 'most' to make Superlative. E.g. easily — more easily — most easily; clearly — more clearly — most clearly; loudly — more loudly — most loudly; quickly — more quickly — most quickly; swiftly — more swiftly — most swiftly; rapidly — more rapidly — most rapidly; wisely — more wisely — most wisely. 3. Some Adverbs have no fixed rule for Comparative and Superlative. E.g. well — better — best; far — farther, further — farthest, furthest; badly — worse — worst; much — more — most; little — less — least. Remember: i. After Comparative Degree, 'than' is used. E.g. (a) 'Karim is better than Rahim.' (b) 'Karim is more intelligent than Rahim.' But after else, other, alternative etc. 'than' is used even though they are not Comparative. E.g. 'He is none else than my brother.', 'She is none other than his sister.' ii. Before Superlative Degree, 'the' is used, and before those among whom the comparison is made, 'of' is used. E.g. 'He is the best of all the boys.', 'Karim is the wisest of all in this village.' iii. To show comparison of one animal or thing of the same class with many animals or things, after Comparative Degree 'than' and then 'any other' or 'all other' is used. E.g. 'The elephant is larger than any other animal or all other animals.' iv. To show comparison of the qualities of the same person or thing, i.e. the difference between two Adjectives, 'more' is placed before the first Adjective, never 'er'. E.g. 'The boy is more strong than tall.' v. To show the better or worse of two, before Comparative Degree 'the' is used and after it, instead of 'than', 'of' is used. E.g. 'He is the better of the two men.', 'Soham is the stronger of the two boys.' vi. In Positive Degree comparison, before the adjective 'as/ so' and after it 'as' is used. E.g. 'He is as brave as a lion.', 'She is as fast as a deer.' vii. After 'than', generally a Pronoun in Nominative case is used (not objective case). E.g. 'Nila is taller than I.', 'Reza is stronger than he.' viii. Sometimes 'Most' only shows that something has a special state or quality in a very high degree. E.g. 'This is a most unfortunate event.', 'It is a most wonderful sight.'

chunk_text: Lesson-01: An Introduction to Article. Read the passage below and notice the underlined words: 'This is Asma Ahmed's bedroom. The room is very neatly made. It has a bed with pillows, cushions, and a colourful, flowery bed-cover. There's a rug in front of the bed with another big cushion. An excellent painting of the sea is hanging from the wall while another small painting is kept on the top of the right side-table. The room has a rocking chair and a sofa at the left corner. The windows are covered with large heavy curtain. Can you see a mask somewhere around the bed?' The underlined words in the passage above are Articles. They sit before a noun or noun-equivalent word to show the definiteness or indefiniteness of the noun. Definition (সংজ্ঞা): Article is such a word that is used before a Noun/ Noun phrase to show the definiteness or indefiniteness of a Noun. [Textbook Focus: English For Today, Page-23 (3.4).] An article is a word that comes before a noun to show whether the noun is specific or not. In English grammar, the articles are 'a, an, and the'. Example: 'In the illustration, there is a man. The man is reading a newspaper. (In the first sentence, a man is not specific but in the second sentence the man is the specific man mentioned in the first sentence.)' In English there are two types of Articles: 1. Definite Article (the): 'The' is used to refer to particular nouns. 2. Indefinite Article (a and an): 'A' and 'An' are used to refer to any noun which is not particular. Remember that, 'a' and 'an' are used only before a singular noun.

chunk_text: Lesson-02: Uses of Articles. Although Articles seem like Adjectives according to their function, they belong to Determiners. As a Determiner, an article gives a hint that a Noun will come after it. There are some differences between Adjective and Article. For example: i. Like Adjective, Article has no Degree of Comparison. ii. Adjective has Predicative use but Articles have no such use. Whether the thing or object we are talking about is known to both the speaker and the listener or unknown, article shows/ expresses that. Articles are used with noun but not all nouns are used with article. So it is necessary to know which noun needs an article and which noun does not need an article, and when needed which article is to be used. [Textbook Focus: English For Today, Page-24 (3.5).] Indefinite Article: 1. 'A' is used before a noun that begins with a consonant sound (e.g., a cat, a pen, etc.) 2. 'An' is generally used before a noun that begins with a vowel sound (e.g., an apple, an egg, etc.). Exceptions: 1. 'A' is used before the vowel 'U' when it is pronounced and sounded as 'You' (e.g., a uniform, a unit, etc.). Similarly 'A' is used before the vowel 'o' when it is pronounced as 'wa'. 2. 'An' is used before a consonant if the first 'h' of a word is silent (e.g., an honest man, an hour, etc.). 3. 'An' is used before some words that begin with consonants but have a vowel sound (e.g. He/she is an M.A.). Definite Article: 1. 'The' is used before specific singular or plural nouns (e.g., I saw a boy in front of the gate. The boy was crying). 2. 'The' is used before a noun that is unique and does not have any alternative to it (e.g., the sun, the earth, etc.). (Note: the book's Textbook Focus box heading prints 'Indefinite Article (নির্দিষ্ট Article)' — the Bangla gloss 'নির্দিষ্ট' (definite) is wrong for Indefinite, which should be 'অনির্দিষ্ট'; the Definite heading correctly says 'নির্দিষ্ট'. chunk_text: Lesson-05: Rules of Articles. i. Use of 'A': 1. Before a countable singular noun beginning with a Consonant, to show indefiniteness indefinite article 'a' is used. E.g. 'This is a dog.', 'It is a picture.' 2. Before all nouns that begin with a Vowel but are pronounced like 'ইউ', 'a' is used. E.g. 'He is a European.', 'This is a university.' 3. When the pronunciation of vowel 'o' is like 'ওয়া', before it indefinite article 'a' is used. E.g. 'I saw a one-eyed man.', 'A one-day cricket match was held here.' 4. Before words of number and measure like couple, dozen, score, hundred, million etc. indefinite article 'a' is used. E.g. 'Hasem bought a dozen oranges.', 'A million people protested against this system.' 5. To show profession or business, indefinite article 'a' is used. E.g. 'She is a nurse.', 'You are a physician.' 6. When Superlative 'most' means 'very', before it 'a' is used instead of 'the'. E.g. 'He saw a most wonderful sight. (a most = a very)', 'This is a most interesting story.' 7. Before the name or title of an unknown person, indefinite article 'a' is used. E.g. 'A Kamol Basu came to see the temple.', 'A Mr. Jenkin has come to see you.' 8. When a Proper Noun is used as a Common Noun in the sense of comparison, before it indefinite article 'a' is used. E.g. 'You are a Kalidas.', 'He thinks he is a Shakespeare.' 9. Sometimes 'a' is used in place of preposition 'on'. Then 'a' is called disguised preposition. E.g. 'The king went a (on) hunting.' 10. Before a Noun, if few, little, good many, lot of, great many, good deal etc. are used, before all those nouns 'a' is used. E.g. 'He has a lot of money.', 'He has read a good deal of books.' ii. Use of 'An': 11. Before an indefinite Countable singular noun or noun phrase whose first letter is a vowel and whose pronunciation is not 'ইউ/ ওয়া', indefinite article 'an' is used. E.g. 'She took an apple.', 'He carried an umbrella.' 12. Even if it begins with a Consonant, if the pronunciation is like a vowel, indefinite article 'an' is used. E.g. 'Mr Rahim is an M.P.', 'Habib is an L.L.B.' 13. In words beginning with 'h', when the pronunciation of 'h' is like 'অ', before those words indefinite article 'an' is used. E.g. 'He is an honest officer.', 'An honourable person will visit our college tomorrow.' iii. Use of 'A'/ 'An': 14. In an exclamatory sentence beginning with What, after what indefinite article 'a/ an' is used. E.g. 'What a beautiful picture it is!', 'What an unhappy man he is!' Note: to show what kind of person/ thing, A/ An is used. E.g. "That's a nice table."

chunk_text: Lesson-01: What is a Verb? Action verb describes physical and mental work. For example — what we do (actions/ what we do), what happens (events/ what happens). Examples: 'Rupom eats a lot of vegetables.', 'He runs every morning.', 'It gives him energy.', 'I saw him in the park.' State verb describes state. For example — what we think (what we think). chunk_text: Lesson-02: 1. Finite Verb (সমাপিকা ক্রিয়া). Definition: the verb that ends the sentence, expresses complete meaning, and whose form is determined by the number and person of the subject of the sentence and by tense, is called a Finite verb. Look at the two sentences below: 'The boy puts on fine clothes.', 'They prepared the document.' In the sentences above, the form of the verb has changed according to the subject — in the first sentence the subject is 3rd person singular, so 's' is added to 'put', and in the second sentence the subject's tense form is past, so '-ed' is added to 'prepare'. Table (Finite verbs / Subject / Tenses / Form of Finite verb): 'I go.' — I: 1st person, Singular — Present — go: 1st Person, singular, present tense; 'You go.' — You: 2nd person, Singular — Present — go: 2nd Person, singular, present tense; 'He go.' — He: 3rd person, Singular — Present — goes: 3rd Person, singular, present tense; 'They go.' — They: 3rd person, Plural — Present — go: 3rd Person, plural, present tense; 'Rupa go.' — Rupa: 3rd person, Singular — Past — went: 3rd person, singular, past tense. chunk_text: Lesson-02: 2. Non-finite Verb (অসমাপিকা ক্রিয়া). Definition: the verb whose form does not change according to the number, person etc. of the subject and which cannot end a sentence is called a Non-finite verb. Look at the sentence below: 'He came to see me.' In this sentence 'came' is a finite verb, because its form has changed according to tense (come → came) and complete meaning is expressed. But 'to see' expresses no complete meaning and there is no tense change according to the subject. Therefore 'to see' is a Non-finite verb. Table (Non-finite verbs / Subject / Tenses / Form of Non-finite Verb): 'I go to play.' / 'You go to play.' / 'He goes to play.' / 'They go to play.' / 'Rupa went to play.' — in every row the non-finite verb stays 'to play' — No Change [কোনো পরিবর্তন হয় না]. Finite Verb is again divided into two parts: i. Principal or Main verb (প্রধান ক্রিয়া) ii. Auxiliary verb (সাহায্যকারী ক্রিয়া). i. Principal Verb/ Main Verb (প্রধান ক্রিয়া). Definition: the verb that independently expresses its own meaning is called a Principal Verb or Main Verb. chunk_text: Lesson-02: ii. Auxiliary verb/ Helping verb (সাহায্যকারী ক্রিয়া). Definition: the verb that helps the principal verb to express complete meaning is called an Auxiliary verb. Look at the sentences below: 'She was waiting for an hour.', 'She had drunk it before we arrived.', 'She is waiting in the library.' If you look, you will see that each underlined word sits before the Principal verb and is used to form continuous tense, negatives and interrogatives. This kind of verb is called auxiliary verb or সাহায্যকারী verb. An Auxiliary verb has no meaning of its own and is used with the principal verb. The number of Auxiliary verbs is 24 in total. They are divided into two parts: i. Primary and ii. Modal. Their Present and Past forms are as follows — Table (Types / Present form / Past form): Primary Auxiliaries — To be: am, is, are / was, were; To do: do, does / did; To have: have, has / had. Modal Auxiliaries (Modals): shall / should; will / would; can / could; may / might; ought to / ×; must / ×; need / ×; dare / ×; × / used to. Auxiliary verb is used: (a) to form Tense: 'He was snoring all night. (Past continuous tense)' (b) to form Negative sentence: 'They are not reading.' (c) to form Interrogative sentence: 'Will you go there?' (d) to form Passive voice: 'The sum is solved by him.' (e) to form Mood: 'I can do it. Did it go well?'
